metadata.title: MacBook Air keyboard replacement, removing rivets
metadata.description:
I did a bunch of searching for methods to remove rivets from a MacBook Air keyboard during the replacement process and could not find a video to show you how. 

I found a method that worked for me and wanted to share it. 

I used these pliers/cutters to remove the rivets. This is a link to Amazon for the set of pliers/cutters that I used, even though I bought my set at Home Depot.


 https://amzn.to/2Jr0cUw

I did get the keyboard to work and wrote these words with my repaired and working MacBook Air. 

My model is a mid-2011 model (A1369). However, this will work for newer models. 

Hope this helps you. 

Preston

summary.brief: A man shows how to pull the rivets out of a MacBook Air keyboard using miniature low‑profile pliers.
summary.detailed: The video begins with the presenter seated on a couch introducing the problem of rivets left in the case after a MacBook Air keyboard removal. He then moves to a kitchen work surface, places the removed keyboard face‑down on a tan countertop, and takes out a Crescent miniature wire cutter and a set of very fine low‑profile pliers. He inserts the tip of the pliers into each rivet, bites down firmly on the rivet head, and leverages the tool upward to pry the rivet free, taking care to keep a solid grip so the pliers do not slip. He repeats the process for every rivet, noting that a few may break or require a bit of smoothing after removal. After all visible rivets are extracted, he briefly discusses handling the case and places the keyboard back onto the case to test its operation.

action.detailed: Grip each rivet with the low‑profile pliers, bite down on the rivet head, and lever upward to pry the rivet free, repeating until all rivets are removed.
action.actor: the man

summary.brief: A man demonstrates how to pull the rivets out of a MacBook Air keyboard using miniature pliers and cutters.
summary.detailed: The video opens with the presenter standing and explaining that rivets remain in the mid‑2011 MacBook Air after the keyboard has been removed. He shows a Crescent miniature wire‑cutter set with fine, low‑profile pliers, then picks up a pair of scissors‑type cutters and inserts the tip into each exposed rivet. By gripping the rivet head, biting the cutter edge into it for leverage, and pulling upward while keeping a solid bite, he extracts the rivet. He repeats the motion for each rivet, warning to keep the pliers from slipping and to use the cutter edge as a focal point when a rivet is difficult. After the last visible rivet is removed, he confirms that all rivets have been taken out.

action.detailed: Grip each rivet with the fine‑profile pliers, bite the cutter edge into the rivet head to create leverage, and pull upward firmly while preventing the tool from slipping, repeating until every rivet is removed.
action.actor: the presenter, a man wearing a light‑blue plaid button‑up shirt

summary.detailed: The presenter places the opened MacBook Air keyboard on a work surface, picks up a red‑handled needle‑nose plier set, and inserts the tips around each exposed rivet. summary.brief: Hands use red‑handled needle‑nose pliers to cut wires and then pry off each key cap from a laptop keyboard.
summary.detailed: The camera stays high and close on a man's hands, which are wearing a blue checkered long‑sleeve shirt. First he wipes dust from the exposed keyboard, then grasps a thin white wire with a red‑handled needle‑nose plier and squeezes to cut it. He repeats the cut on a black wire at the lower‑left corner and also trims a thin cord that is taped to a small piece. After the wires are removed, he shifts the pliers to the keyboard itself, positioning the jaws around the edge of a key cap, levering upward to pop the cap free. He moves the tool like a pencil along each key, adjusting his hand to reach harder‑to‑access caps, and repeats the prying motion until all visible key caps are detached. The sequence runs in fast‑motion and concludes with a brief black screen.

action.detailed: Grip each wire or key cap with the red‑handled needle‑nose pliers, apply cutting or levering pressure to detach it, and repeat across the keyboard until all wires are cut and all key caps are pried off.

summary_sent_to_llm.title: MacBook Air keyboard replacement, removing rivets
summary_sent_to_llm.description:
I did a bunch of searching for methods to remove rivets from a MacBook Air keyboard during the replacement process and could not find a video to show you how. 

I found a method that worked for me and wanted to share it. 

I used these pliers/cutters to remove the rivets. This is a link to Amazon for the set of pliers/cutters that I used, even though I bought my set at Home Depot.


 https://amzn.to/2Jr0cUw

I did get the keyboard to work and wrote these words with my repaired and working MacBook Air. 

My model is a mid-2011 model (A1369). However, this will work for newer models. 

Hope this
summary_sent_to_llm.root_summary: The video begins with the presenter seated on a couch introducing the problem of rivets left in the case after a MacBook Air keyboard removal. He then moves to a kitchen work surface, places the removed keyboard face‑down on a tan countertop, and takes out a Crescent miniature wire cutter and a set of very fine low‑profile pliers. He inserts the tip of the pliers into each rivet, bites down firmly on the rivet head, and leverages the tool upward to pry the rivet free, taking care to keep a solid grip so the pliers do not slip. He repeats the process for every rivet, noting that a few may break or require a bit of smoothing after removal. After all visible rivets are extracted, he briefly discusses handling the case and places the keyboard back onto the case to test its operation.
action_list: Demonstrate cutter package and reveal keyboard
Display and set down tool package
Pry and remove small keyboard parts with pliers

llm.system_prompt:
You evaluate YouTube videos for a video-understanding benchmark.

You will be given an Action100M-style summary of one video: title, description,
a hierarchical GPT-written summary of the whole video, and a deduplicated list
of action labels extracted at multiple levels of the video.

Your job is to judge:

1) DOMAINS — does this video clearly belong to any of these target domains?
   - "kitchen": a person preparing food in a kitchen-like setting
     (cooking, baking, food prep — NOT eating reviews, NOT pet-food prep,
     NOT food-product unboxing, NOT restaurant vlogs).
   - "manipulation": a person performing hand-object manipulation tasks
     with clear physical goals: assembly/disassembly, repair, crafting,
     tool use, packing, sorting. The video must show clear procedural
     manipulation, NOT just incidental hand movement (e.g. a vlog where
     someone holds things while talking does NOT count).
   - "navigation": the camera moves through a physical environment as an
     agent traverses space — first-person walking tours (museum, store,
     home, city street), driving / cycling / hiking POV footage, drone
     fly-throughs of indoor or outdoor scenes, room/house walkthroughs.
     The camera's translation through the environment IS the main content.
     Does NOT count: a stationary tripod with someone talking; a tutorial
     filmed in one place; b-roll where the camera only pans or zooms but
     does not translate; sports footage where the player moves but the
     camera stays put.
   A video can match zero, one, or multiple domains. Be strict — when in
   doubt, say "neither".

2) NUM_DISTINCT_EVENTS — count the number of *semantically distinct*
   sub-events (procedural steps) you see in the action list. Merge
   paraphrases of the same step into one. Ignore generic narration steps
   like "speak to camera" or "display title".

3) IS_GOOD_CANDIDATE — true only if BOTH:
   - at least one target domain matches
   - num_distinct_events > 3 (the video shows a real multi-step procedure)

Always return strict JSON in the requested schema.
